ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Addiction Medicine Consultation — Elvis Presley — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: One-week review, seen the same day by addiction medicine: diagnoses, buprenorphine started in the office, the benzodiazepines combined into one, the sleep study and home blood pressure results

text.paragraph: Long-term prescription opioids and benzodiazepines from five prescribers, with fatigue, weight gain, constipation, daytime sleepiness and high blood pressure, in a 39-year-old touring singer who wants to change how he takes his medicines. Please assess for substance use disorders and advise on medication for opioid use disorder and a safe benzodiazepine plan. [S]
Urgency: Within one week, on the day of his one-week primary care review, at his request before a Las Vegas engagement in five weeks. [S]

list.item: Does he meet DSM-5-TR criteria for opioid and sedative use disorders, and how severe?
Should he start buprenorphine, and how: in the office or at home, standard or low-dose start?
How should the two benzodiazepines be managed alongside buprenorphine, and at what taper pace?
What monitoring do you advise (urine testing, monitoring program, visit frequency, naloxone)?
How should care be planned around a Las Vegas engagement and a tour this autumn?

text.paragraph: Mr. Presley, a 39-year-old singer, is seen at the request of Dr. Ashby-Nakagawa. He began opioids about five years ago for back and neck pain from performing, and benzodiazepines for sleep after late shows. Over time he took more than prescribed, found more than one prescriber, and felt sick and craved them when he ran short; a hospital stay some years ago withdrew him from opioids, and he restarted within months. He has never injected or used illicit drugs and does not drink. For the past week he has taken only this clinic's prescriptions. He last took hydromorphone about 18 hours ago and oxycodone about 20 hours ago, as planned, and is in mild to moderate withdrawal. He took diazepam and alprazolam last night. He has a Las Vegas engagement in five weeks and a tour after it and wants to start treatment now. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Elvis Aron Presley was born in a two-room house in Tupelo, Mississippi, on January 8, 1935; his family moved to Memphis when he was 13. [D]

He made his first record in 1953, became a national star in 1956, served in the Army in West Germany from 1958 to 1960, and by the 1970s performed long engagements in Las Vegas and toured constantly. In 1974 he played Las Vegas from January 26 to February 9, toured through much of March, including four shows in Memphis on March 16 and 17 and a recorded show there on March 20, played Lake Tahoe from May 16 to 26, toured again in mid-June, and took a few weeks off at Graceland from early July. [D]

From October 15 to November 1, 1973, he was treated at Baptist Memorial Hospital in Memphis under an assumed name; at the 1981 trial of his physician, an internal medicine specialist who reviewed the records testified that the consulting physicians were "withdrawing him from narcotic drugs." [D]
He had glaucoma, including an episode of acute angle-closure glaucoma in 1971, and was under the care of one ophthalmologist from 1971 on. [D]
It was believed that he neither smoked nor drank alcohol. [D]

text.paragraph: No results recorded at this visit.

list.item: Opioid use disorder, severe (F11.20). Seven DSM-5-TR criteria: larger amounts than intended, unsuccessful efforts to cut down, much time spent obtaining prescriptions, craving, continued use despite physical problems, tolerance and withdrawal, which count here because the opioids were not taken as prescribed. Buprenorphine lowers the risk of overdose and death and fits a touring life better than methadone, which needs daily clinic dosing. A standard start is suitable because his opioids are short-acting and he is already in moderate withdrawal; a low-dose start would be chosen for someone who cannot tolerate withdrawal or is on methadone. [S]

Sedative, hypnotic, or anxiolytic use disorder (benzodiazepines), moderate (F13.20). Five criteria, including withdrawal. Abrupt stopping risks seizures. The 1973 joint guideline allows a switch to a single longer-acting benzodiazepine, advises against tapering during other major changes, and suggests reductions of about 5 to 10% every two to four weeks, adjusted to symptoms. Taking a benzodiazepine is not a reason to withhold buprenorphine, but the combination raises the risk of sedation and slowed breathing, especially with sleep apnea. [S]

Obstructive sleep apnea (G47.33). Moderate obstructive sleep apnea with a small central component; CPAP is important while he takes buprenorphine and diazepam, and no additional night sedative should be used. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Ashby-Nakagawa's intake note and the prescription drug monitoring program report (five prescribers, three pharmacies, about 145 MME a day with two benzodiazepines). DAST-10 7, AUDIT-C 0, PHQ-9 8, GAD-7 9. The structured safety assessment. Liver tests mildly raised; ECG normal with a QTc of 436 ms. In-laboratory polysomnography three days ago: apnea-hypopnea index 26 an hour, central apnea index 4. Point-of-care urine test today: hydromorphone, oxycodone and benzodiazepines; no fentanyl. COWS 12. [S]

list.item: Start buprenorphine with naloxone in the office today at COWS 12: 4 mg, then 4 mg after an hour if withdrawal persists; 16 mg daily from tomorrow, adjusted up to 24 mg for cravings or withdrawal. [S]
Stop hydromorphone and oxycodone today and take back the remaining tablets; no full-agonist opioid from any prescriber. [S]

Combine diazepam and alprazolam into diazepam 10 mg four times daily (40 mg a day); no taper step until buprenorphine has been stable for two to three weeks, then reduce by about 10% every four weeks or so, pausing for engagements, illness or withdrawal symptoms; CBT for anxiety and insomnia. [S]
Naloxone at home and in the tour bag, with people around him trained; no alcohol, no other sedatives, and CPAP every night. [S]

A single prescriber and one named pharmacy, a monitoring program check before each prescription, seven-day supplies for the first month then two weeks, and a urine drug test at the start, about a month later and when doses change. [S]
Weekly contact for the first month, counseling, and safety review at every visit. [S]
For engagements and tours: no medication change in the week before, prescriptions sent to one named pharmacy where he will be, weekly video visits, and a written plan for missed doses. [S]
For acute pain: continue buprenorphine and split the dose, add an NSAID or other non-opioid treatment, and call this clinic before any other prescriber gives an opioid. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Ashby-Nakagawa, who saw him the same day. The diagnoses and the plan were explained to Mr. Presley without blame; he asked whether buprenorphine would affect his voice or his energy on stage, was told that it should not once the dose is steady, and chose to start today. [S]

Follow-up: Addiction medicine will see him again in three months or sooner if cravings return or the taper stalls; Dr. Ashby-Nakagawa prescribes and follows him, with weekly contact in the first month. [S]
